api.name: defineApp / Application
api.summary: Define pages, socket routes and application services together. Nothing listens until run(); one owner starts and stops the shared HTTP/WebSocket listener.
options: pages: decorated page classes (default [])
sockets: SocketRoute classes (default [])
services: application-wide classes with onInit(app, signal) and onShutdown() (default [])
port: number (default 8181); use 0 for an ephemeral test port
bind: string (default 0.0.0.0)
httpServices: existing Express service descriptors; route-specific SocketService classes remain on socket routes
startupTimeoutMs / shutdownTimeoutMs: total lifecycle budgets (default 5000 each)
signals: install owned process signal handling when run begins (default true); embedded applications/tests can set false
Existing live-page/HTTP options, including templateRoot, authentication, origins, server (Express app), development and ssl
Static export remains exportStatic(); defineApp does not accept a static export flag

methods.name: defineApp(options) / new Application(options)
methods.detail: Create a deferred definition. Registration arrays are copied; imports and definitions open no port or process handlers.

methods.name: run(): Promise<Application>
methods.detail: Initialize services in order and bind one HTTP/WS listener. Repeated calls share startup while running. A stopped application cannot restart.

methods.name: shutdown(): Promise<void>
methods.detail: Cancel pending startup and perform bounded, idempotent cleanup. Close HTTP/socket resources before releasing application services in reverse order. Preserve cleanup errors.

methods.name: options
methods.detail: Copied definition, available for defining independent test applications with port: 0 and signals: false. Captured objects and supplied Express apps are not deep-cloned.

methods.name: app / server / http / sockets / services
methods.detail: Runtime Express application, native listener, HTTP adapter, optional WebSocket server and service instances. HTTP members are null before startup; await run before use.

methods.name: revoke(principal): Promise<number>
methods.detail: Revoke matching live-page sessions; zero before live pages have been initialized.

methods.name: inspect(): DevelopmentSnapshot | null
methods.detail: Return opt-in live-page inspection metadata, or null when unavailable/disabled.

article.eli5: One front door serves pages and ongoing socket conversations. The application prepares its staff before opening that door, then closes the door and sends the staff home in order.
article.useWhen: Use it as the entry point for a multi-page site, a realtime UI, a routed socket backend, or their combination. Lower-level server classes remain available for custom ownership.
walkthrough: Declare pages with decorators and socket routes with message-type handlers, then register their classes in one definition.
Acquire app-wide resources in service onInit(app, signal), not constructors. onInit can register Express endpoints through app.app before listening.

Await run to know startup succeeded; no separately stored HTTP server or second socket startup call is necessary. CommonJS entry points use an async function or handle the returned promise; top-level await requires a suitable ESM configuration.
For tests, use an ephemeral port, disable process signal ownership and await shutdown in cleanup. The generated applications ship real HTTP/socket and process tests.
article.watchFor: This is lifecycle composition, not dependency injection or durable/distributed state. Services must cooperate with cancellation and release partially acquired resources. Deadlines cannot interrupt synchronous event-loop blocking. Shared page-class closure objects stay shared; use separate classes/rooms when isolation is required.

api.name: HttpServer
api.summary: Lower-level Express HTTP listener with parsers, CORS, static assets and services. Prefer defineApp for new applications; use HttpServer when you explicitly need its immediately listening constructor or custom listener ownership.
options: port: number (default 80)
bind: string (default 0.0.0.0)
publicPaths: string[] (default ["./public"])
services: array of { serviceName, method, function }
listen: boolean (default true); set false to build app without binding a port
listenCallback: function invoked after listen
encoding: "json" | "urlencoded" (default json)
corsOptions: passed to cors

methods.name: constructor(options)
methods.detail: Merges defaults, wires body parsing, CORS, static serving, registers REST services, and starts listening unless listen is false.

methods.name: app (Express instance)
methods.detail: Use the returned `app` to add middleware or routes exactly like a normal Express server.

article.eli5: Think of HttpServer as a furnished storefront: Express is the building, while Redweb installs the front door, service counter, signs, and sensible safety rails before you open.
article.useWhen: Choose it when Redweb should own a normal HTTP listener and you still want direct access to Express for middleware or one-off routes.
walkthrough: Redweb creates the Express application and installs the configured parsers, CORS policy, static folders, and services.
The server binds to the requested interface unless listen is false.
The app property remains the same Express application, so adding /health does not require a Redweb abstraction.
article.watchFor: Use listen: false when another object must own the Node listener; two owners trying to bind the same port is an application design error.

api.name: BaseHttpServer
api.summary: Public Express app builder used by HttpServer and HttpsServer. Use it for advanced composition when you want Redweb middleware, static files, and services without any listener behavior.
options: All `HttpServer` app-building options
server: existing Express application to configure
listen is ignored because BaseHttpServer never binds a port

methods.name: constructor(options)
methods.detail: Builds or configures an Express app with body parsing, CORS, static serving, and REST services.

methods.name: app (Express instance)
methods.detail: The configured Express application. Pass it to http.createServer(app) for custom server ownership.

article.eli5: BaseHttpServer prepares the kitchen but does not open the restaurant. You get a fully arranged Express app and decide which Node server will serve it.
article.useWhen: Use it for custom composition, tests, serverless adapters, or any setup where creating and listening on the HTTP server belongs to your application.
walkthrough: The constructor configures either your Express app or a new one.
Static folders and service definitions are registered in deterministic order.
You pass base.app to http.createServer, a test harness, or another host when you are ready.
article.watchFor: It intentionally ignores listener settings. If requests are not arriving, confirm that your own server is listening and forwarding them to base.app.

api.name: HttpsServer
api.summary: TLS-enabled variant of `HttpServer`. Accepts `ssl.key` and `ssl.cert` file paths, wraps them in an https server, and bootstraps the same middleware pipeline.
options: All `HttpServer` options
ssl.key: path to private key (required)
ssl.cert: path to certificate (required)

methods.name: constructor(options)
methods.detail: Loads the provided key/cert pair, builds the Express app with BaseHttpServer, then creates and starts the HTTPS listener unless listen is false.

article.eli5: HttpsServer is HttpServer with a locked, encrypted front door. It reads your certificate and key, then serves the same Express application through TLS.
article.useWhen: Use it when the Node process terminates TLS itself instead of sitting behind a reverse proxy or managed load balancer.
walkthrough: The key and certificate files are loaded before the listener starts.
The standard HTTP middleware and services are attached to the Express app.
The resulting HTTPS server binds on the configured port and handles encrypted requests.
article.watchFor: Certificate rotation, filesystem permissions, and secure protocol policy remain deployment concerns. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, HttpServer is usually simpler.

api.name: SocketServer
api.summary: HTTP-upgrade WebSocket server on top of `ws`. Builds and listens on its own HTTP server by default; if you pass a Node `server`, it attaches upgrade handling and leaves `.listen()` to you unless `listen: true` is explicit.
options: port: number (default 3000)
listen: boolean (default true for owned servers); supplied servers do not listen unless explicitly true
server: existing http.Server to attach to without double-listening (optional)
routes: array of SocketRoute subclasses (defaults to a single DefaultRoute at "/")

methods.name: constructor(options)
methods.detail: Creates or reuses an HTTP server, instantiates supplied routes or a DefaultRoute, attaches upgrade handling, and starts listening only when Redweb owns the server or listen is explicitly true.

methods.name: addRoute(RouteClass)
methods.detail: Instantiate and register another `SocketRoute` at runtime.

methods.name: handleUpgrade(req, socket, head)
methods.detail: Internal: normalises the request path, picks a matching route (or "/"), and forwards the upgrade to that route's server.

methods.name: shutdown()
methods.detail: Closes all registered routes and the underlying HTTP server.

article.eli5: SocketServer is a switchboard for persistent conversations. It accepts a WebSocket upgrade, finds the route for that path, and lets that route handle the connection.
article.useWhen: Use defineApp({ sockets: [ChatRoute] }) for normal startup. Use SocketServer directly to attach routed upgrades to a separately owned Node HTTP server.
walkthrough: The HTTP server is built or reused according to the options.
Upgrade requests are matched to routes instead of being sent to every handler.
Each route owns its clients, handlers, services, limits, and cleanup lifecycle.
article.watchFor: When supplying an existing Node server, Redweb does not assume it should call listen. Make listener ownership explicit and shut down in the reverse order of startup.

api.name: SecureSocketServer
api.summary: HTTPS + WebSocket pairing. Mirrors `SocketServer`, creating an owned HTTPS server from TLS files or attaching to a supplied HTTPS server.
api.usage:
import { SecureSocketServer } from 'redweb'
import { GameRoute } from './routes/GameRoute.js'

new SecureSocketServer({
  port: 3443,
  ssl: { key: './certs/dev.key', cert: './certs/dev.crt' },
  routes: [GameRoute],
})
options: port: number (default 3000)
listen: boolean (default true for owned servers); supplied servers do not listen unless explicitly true
server: existing https.Server to attach to without double-listening (optional)
ssl.key and ssl.cert: required file paths only when creating an owned HTTPS server
closeServerOnShutdown: defaults to true for owned servers and false for supplied servers
routes: array of SocketRoute subclasses

methods.name: constructor(options)
methods.detail: Loads TLS files or reuses a supplied HTTPS server, registers the provided routes, attaches upgrade handling, and starts listening only when Redweb owns the server or listen is explicitly true.

methods.name: addRoute(RouteClass)
methods.detail: Same runtime route attachment as `SocketServer`.

methods.name: shutdown()
methods.detail: Stops routes and services. Closes the HTTPS listener only when owned or closeServerOnShutdown is explicitly true; supplied servers remain open by default.

article.eli5: SecureSocketServer is the encrypted version of the WebSocket switchboard: clients use wss:// and the connection stays protected from the first handshake onward.
article.useWhen: Use it to own a TLS WebSocket listener or share an existing Node HTTPS server.
walkthrough: TLS material is loaded when creating an owned listener; a supplied HTTPS server already owns its TLS configuration and needs no ssl file options.
WebSocket upgrades travel through the same route selection used by SocketServer.
Route handlers see ordinary Redweb sockets after the secure handshake completes.
article.watchFor: Supplied HTTPS servers remain open after shutdown by default; their owner controls listening and final cleanup. Do not duplicate TLS termination accidentally: behind a TLS-terminating proxy, use SocketServer and configure trusted origins.

api.name: SocketRoute
api.summary: Defines a WebSocket endpoint and owns its handlers, services, clients, and opt-in multiplayer policies. Routes can add bounded admission, transport limits, ordered work, heartbeat, rooms, resumable sessions, distribution, draining, metrics, and protocol negotiation without changing legacy routes.
options: path: WebSocket path (required)
handlers: array of handler classes (required)
services: array of SocketService subclasses (optional)
allowDuplicateConnections: allow multiple clients from the same IP

websocketOptions: options passed to ws WebSocketServer, such as maxPayload or perMessageDeflate; closeTimeout defaults to 5000 milliseconds (integer 1..2147483647) and bounds an already-started closing handshake, not healthy idle connections
admission: authenticate, validate origins, and optionally place a client before upgrade
maxPendingUpgrades: finite concurrent admission/negotiation work (default 64)
limits: connection, message-rate, pending-message, and outbound-buffer ceilings
orderedMessages: serialize each connection through a bounded queue
heartbeat: one route-level half-open connection monitor
rooms and sessions: bounded grouping and expiring application-issued ownership
distribution: optional bounded broker adapter; no broker is bundled or required
drainHandlers: track handler work and expose a cooperative shutdown signal
protocol: version negotiation, stable envelopes/error codes, and optional binary codecs
connections: optional connectedClients group for verified player facades and private page projection; enables rooms and handler draining by default

methods.name: constructor({ path, handlers, services, allowDuplicateConnections, websocketOptions })
methods.detail: Validates input, instantiates handlers/services, sets up a `ws` server for the path with any websocketOptions, and registers connection listeners.

methods.name: addHandler(HandlerClass)
methods.detail: Adds another handler class unless a handler with the same name already exists.

methods.name: handleConnection(socket, req)
methods.detail: Stores the client (deduping by IP unless allowed), decorates the socket with `sendJson`/`broadcast`, and wires close/error/message listeners.

methods.name: handleMessage(socket, data)
methods.detail: Dispatches an already-parsed message object by type. Only literal false declines success; a deliberate rejection should send a correlated protocol error. Unexpected handler exceptions retain sanitized failure and connection-close behavior.

methods.name: handleBinaryMessage(socket, buffer)
methods.detail: Handles binary frames separately from JSON text frames and delegates to a handler selected by acceptsBinary(socket, buffer).

methods.name: handleClose(socket, ip)
methods.detail: Removes the client from the registry and triggers an optional `connectionCloseCallback`.

methods.name: shutdown()
methods.detail: Marks the route draining, stops services, bounds handler/adapter cleanup, closes clients, and releases every route-owned resource.

methods.name: beginDrain()
methods.detail: Flips readiness and rejects new upgrades before shutdown work begins.

methods.name: isReady()
methods.detail: Reports whether the route is accepting upgrades and any required distribution adapter is healthy.

methods.name: publish(type, payload)
methods.detail: Publishes through the optional bounded distribution adapter and resolves to a success boolean.

methods.name: handleError(socket, error, ip)
methods.detail: Logs socket errors; override for custom reporting.

article.eli5: A SocketRoute is a room with its own door and rules. The URL chooses the room; message.type chooses which handler inside the room receives the message.
article.useWhen: Create one whenever a WebSocket path represents a distinct protocol, trust boundary, workload, or group of multiplayer resources.
walkthrough: The /chat path selects this route during the WebSocket upgrade.
Admission and capacity checks run before the connection becomes an active client.
Messages are dispatched by type to BaseHandler instances while route services and registries share the same lifecycle.
article.watchFor: Keep routing decisions out of message.action branches. Prefer one route per protocol area and one handler per message type.

api.name: SocketService
api.summary: Route-scoped background worker. Used by `SocketRoute` to run ticks or lifecycle hooks tied to a specific route.

methods.name: constructor(name, tickRateMs = null)
methods.detail: Stores a service id and optional tick interval; the interval is activated in onInit if onTick exists.

methods.name: onInit(route)
methods.detail: Called once by SocketRoute, sets `this.route` and, if a tick interval was supplied, schedules recurring onTick execution.

methods.name: onTick()
methods.detail: Optional; implement to run on the configured interval.

methods.name: onShutdown()
methods.detail: Clears the tick interval; extend for cleanup hooks.

article.eli5: A SocketService is a helper that clocks in when its route starts and clocks out when the route stops, such as presence tracking or a periodic snapshot publisher.
article.useWhen: Use it for route-scoped background behavior that needs explicit startup, shutdown, and access to the owning route.
walkthrough: SocketRoute constructs and initializes the service through onInit(route).
The optional tick interval invokes onTick; simple SocketService ticks do not await earlier asynchronous ticks.
onShutdown releases the interval; overrides must also release their application resources and call the base cleanup.
article.watchFor: Use onInit/onShutdown, not start/stop hooks. Use FixedStepService for non-overlapping async ticks and bounded catch-up; plain SocketService does not provide those guarantees.

api.name: FixedStepService
api.summary: Route-scoped simulation clock that compensates for drift, prevents overlapping async ticks, bounds catch-up work, and reports dropped retained lag instead of replaying forever.

methods.name: constructor(name, tickRateMs, maxCatchUpTicks?, maxRetainedLagMs?)
methods.detail: Creates a fixed-step route service with finite catch-up and retained-lag limits.

methods.name: onTick(stepMs, tick)
methods.detail: Implement one simulation step. Async work never overlaps the next pulse.

methods.name: onLagDropped(milliseconds)
methods.detail: Optional observability hook called when retained lag is deliberately discarded.

article.eli5: FixedStepService is a metronome for game logic. Even when the computer hesitates, it advances the simulation in measured beats without starting two beats at once.
article.useWhen: Use it for authoritative simulations or periodic work that needs stable step sizes, bounded catch-up, and explicit handling of excessive lag.
walkthrough: The service schedules ticks using the configured fixed interval.
A slow asynchronous tick finishes before another begins.
Limited catch-up reduces drift, while old excess lag is reported and discarded instead of causing an endless spiral.
article.watchFor: A fixed step does not make expensive work free. Measure onTick duration, set conservative catch-up limits, and keep network I/O outside the critical simulation path.

api.name: RoomRegistry
api.summary: Bounded route-local connection groups. Use asynchronous enterRoom for guarded membership, joinRoom for unguarded rooms, and roomBroadcast for delivery; disconnect cleanup removes all memberships and reclaims empty rooms.

methods.name: socket.joinRoom(roomId)
methods.detail: Idempotently joins an unguarded bounded room and returns whether membership is active. Throws when rooms.authorize is configured; use await socket.enterRoom(roomId) instead.

methods.name: await socket.enterRoom(roomId)
methods.detail: Applies configured room authorization before committing bounded membership and resolves to whether membership is active. Also works for unguarded rooms.

methods.name: registry.roomsFor(socket)
methods.detail: Returns a snapshot of the socket's current room IDs. Room membership is delivery state, not a durable game seat.

methods.name: socket.leaveRoom(roomId)
methods.detail: Idempotently leaves one room and reclaims it when empty.

methods.name: socket.roomBroadcast(roomId, data, options?)
methods.detail: Serializes once and sends to selected connected members.

article.eli5: RoomRegistry is a set of labeled group chats. A socket can join a label, and one message can be delivered to everyone carrying that label.
article.useWhen: Use rooms for match participants, parties, regions, spectators, or any bounded route-local fan-out group.
walkthrough: A join handler awaits socket.enterRoom(roomId) for protected rooms and checks the result before treating entry as accepted.
The move handler broadcasts the accepted update to that room and can exclude the sender.
Disconnect cleanup removes every membership and empty rooms are reclaimed automatically.
article.watchFor: A room is a delivery group, not authoritative game state. Validate membership and permissions before broadcasting, and configure hard room and membership limits.

api.name: SessionRegistry
api.summary: Bounded, expiring ownership records for application-issued opaque session IDs. Redweb handles takeover and expiry; the application owns credential issuance and payload validation.

methods.name: socket.createSession(sessionId, data)
methods.detail: Creates a bounded application-issued session owned by the current connection.

methods.name: socket.resumeSession(sessionId)
methods.detail: Atomically transfers ownership, closes the former owner, and returns stored data.

methods.name: stop()
methods.detail: Stops the one route-level sweep timer and clears every retained record.

article.eli5: SessionRegistry is a numbered coat-check ticket. A reconnecting player presents the ticket and safely takes ownership of the stored session from an older connection.
article.useWhen: Use it for short reconnect windows, controlled connection takeover, and small pieces of application-issued resumable state.
walkthrough: The application creates an opaque session ID and stores bounded state against the connected socket.
After a disconnect, the record remains available for the configured TTL.
Resume atomically transfers ownership and closes the former owner if it is still connected.
article.watchFor: Session IDs are credentials: issue them securely, never trust client-selected identity, limit stored data, and persist important state outside this in-memory registry.

api.name: ProtocolClient
api.summary: Low-level envelope helper from redweb/client. It wraps a socket you own; it does not connect, reconnect or correlate pending requests. For those features use redweb-client; server TSX pages generate their client integration automatically.

methods.name: constructor(socket, version)
methods.detail: Wraps any socket-like object with send(data) and selects the envelope version.

methods.name: envelope(type, payload, metadata?)
methods.detail: Builds a stable versioned event with optional requestId and sequence.

methods.name: send(type, payload, metadata?)
methods.detail: Serializes and sends one versioned event through the wrapped socket.

methods.name: parse(value)
methods.detail: Parses and validates a protocol event or error envelope.

article.eli5: ProtocolClient is a phrasebook shared with the browser. It puts outgoing messages into Redweb’s expected envelope and checks incoming envelopes before your code trusts them.
article.useWhen: Use it when you already own the connection and only need versioned envelopes. Use redweb-client for connection lifecycle and requests, or typed handlers bound to server TSX for generated UI transport.
walkthrough: Create a WebSocket and its envelope helper, then wait for open before sending.
send builds a stable typed envelope containing payload and optional sequence metadata.
parse validates server messages so application code can respond to known errors such as rate limiting.
article.watchFor: Bundle this import for browser use; it is not a native script URL. Envelope validation is not payload validation or authorization, and this helper does not replay messages after disconnect.

api.name: SocketRegistry
api.summary: Small EventEmitter-backed list for socket-scoped entities (players, rooms, etc.). Emits `added` and `removed` events.
api.usage:
import { SocketRegistry } from 'redweb'

const players = new SocketRegistry()
players.on('added', player => console.log('Joined:', player.id))
players.add({ id: 'alice' })
players.remove('alice')

methods.name: add(item)
methods.detail: Stores the item and emits an `added` event.

methods.name: remove(itemOrId, by = "id")
methods.detail: Remove by object reference or by matching a property (defaults to "id"); returns true when removal occurred and emits `removed`.

methods.name: all()
methods.detail: Returns a shallow copy of all stored items.

methods.name: count()
methods.detail: Convenience getter for `all().length`.

article.eli5: SocketRegistry is a list with a doorbell: add or remove an item and interested code receives an event.
article.useWhen: Use it for simple application-managed collections with added/removed events. Use RoomRegistry for bounded socket membership or connectedClients for page projections.
walkthrough: add stores an item and emits added; duplicate items are not rejected.
remove matches an object by identity or an identifier by the chosen property, then emits removed.
all returns a shallow array copy. The application owns limits and cleanup.
article.watchFor: This registry is unbounded and is not SocketRoute.clients. It does not automatically register connections, remove disconnected sockets, or drain them.

api.name: BaseHandler
api.summary: Abstract message handler. Provide a name in the constructor; clients send `{ type: name, ... }` to target JSON messages, while binary frames can be accepted and handled as raw Buffer payloads.

methods.name: constructor(name)
methods.detail: Stores the handler name used by incoming messages.

methods.name: handleMessage(socket, message)
methods.detail: Calls onMessage; override only if you need pre/post handling logic.

methods.name: onMessage(socket, message)
methods.detail: Required; implement your message processing here. Throwing will close the socket with an error.

methods.name: acceptsBinary(socket, buffer)
methods.detail: Optional selector used by SocketRoute to choose a handler for binary frames. Return true when this handler should receive the Buffer.

methods.name: handleBinaryMessage(socket, buffer)
methods.detail: Calls onBinaryMessage. If onBinaryMessage is not implemented, Redweb sends a "Binary messages are not supported by this handler" error.

methods.name: onBinaryMessage(socket, buffer)
methods.detail: Optional; override for normal binary-message handling. The second argument is the raw Buffer payload.

methods.name: onInitialContact(socket)
methods.detail: Optional hook for first-touch logic (not used by default route).

article.eli5: BaseHandler is a labeled mailbox. A message with the matching type goes directly into that mailbox, so your code does not need a switch statement.
article.useWhen: Create a small handler for each message type that deserves its own validation, authorization, rate policy, and behavior.
walkthrough: The handler name declares the message type it accepts.
SocketRoute performs dispatch before onMessage runs.
The handler validates the payload, changes authoritative state, and sends or broadcasts the result.
article.watchFor: Do not add a second message.action dispatcher inside one handler. That hides protocol operations and defeats type-based routing.

api.name: sendJson
api.summary: Low-level JSON serialization/send helper. Inside a route, prefer socket.sendJson() so the route’s outbound policy is applied.

methods.name: sendJson(socket, data)
methods.detail: Serialises data and writes it to the socket.

article.eli5: sendJson is a careful packer: give it a JavaScript value and it turns that value into one JSON message before placing it on the socket.
article.useWhen: Use it for structured server-to-client messages instead of repeating JSON.stringify and transport checks throughout handlers.
walkthrough: Inside a handler, socket.sendJson uses the route’s outbound checks.
Standalone sendJson(socket, data) serializes and sends without inheriting a route policy.
A true result means the send was accepted locally, not that a peer received it.
article.watchFor: The standalone helper can throw on serialization or transport failure. It does not automatically apply route backpressure. Bound payloads and use the route-bound helper when available.

api.name: ERROR_CODES
api.summary: Stable framework error codes shared by protocol-enabled servers and redweb/client.

methods.name: Message errors
methods.detail: INVALID_MESSAGE, UNKNOWN_HANDLER, HANDLER_FAILED, and BINARY_UNSUPPORTED.

methods.name: Capacity errors
methods.detail: RATE_LIMITED, QUEUE_FULL, and CAPACITY_REACHED.

methods.name: Lifecycle errors
methods.detail: INITIALIZATION_FAILED.

article.eli5: ERROR_CODES is a shared list of machine-readable reasons, like standardized traffic signs that every client interprets the same way.
article.useWhen: Use these constants whenever application behavior depends on a Redweb protocol failure rather than human-facing wording.
walkthrough: The server emits a stable code inside its error envelope.
The client compares it with ERROR_CODES instead of copying a string literal.
UI or retry policy can change independently of the readable error message.
article.watchFor: Codes describe protocol outcomes, not every domain failure. Add your own namespaced application codes without changing Redweb’s meanings.

api.name: SOCKET_OPTIONS
api.summary: Default WebSocket server options used by BaseSocketServer.
api.usage:
import { SOCKET_OPTIONS } from 'redweb'
// { port: 3000, ssl: null, listen: true, routes: [] }

methods.name: port
methods.detail: Default WebSocket port (3000).

methods.name: ssl
methods.detail: Default TLS config (null).

methods.name: listen
methods.detail: Owned socket servers listen by default. Supplied servers remain caller-owned unless listen is explicitly true.

methods.name: routes
methods.detail: Routes array default (empty; a DefaultRoute is created when none are provided).

article.eli5: SOCKET_OPTIONS is the default settings card Redweb starts from before applying the socket choices you provide.
article.useWhen: Read it to understand defaults or build tooling that presents Redweb configuration, but pass explicit options for production decisions.
walkthrough: Redweb begins with immutable documented defaults.
User configuration overrides only the supplied fields.
The normalized result is used consistently when the socket server starts.
article.watchFor: Treat exported defaults as documentation, not mutable global configuration. Never change the object to configure one server.

api.name: HTTP_OPTIONS
api.summary: Frozen defaults used by the HTTP and HTTPS server constructors.

methods.name: Server defaults
methods.detail: port, bind, listen, ssl, logger, and static public paths.

methods.name: Application defaults
methods.detail: services, encoding, CORS, and safe error exposure.

article.eli5: HTTP_OPTIONS is Redweb’s starter checklist for HTTP servers: port, bind address, public folders, encoding, and related defaults.
article.useWhen: Consult it when you need to know what omitted HttpServer options mean or when generating configuration documentation.
walkthrough: The server copies its baseline HTTP choices.
Your provided values are validated and merged.
The completed configuration drives app creation and optional listener startup.
article.watchFor: Defaults are convenient locally but production networking should be explicit, especially bind address, port, CORS, and listener ownership.

api.name: ENCODINGS
api.summary: Supported request-body parser names for HTTP server configuration.
api.usage:
import { ENCODINGS } from 'redweb'
// ENCODINGS.json, ENCODINGS.urlencoded

methods.name: json
methods.detail: Use Express JSON body parsing.

methods.name: urlencoded
methods.detail: Use Express URL-encoded body parsing.

article.eli5: ENCODINGS is a tiny menu that lets you choose whether request bodies arrive as JSON or traditional URL-encoded form data.
article.useWhen: Use the constants when configuring HTTP body parsing so spelling stays aligned with supported Redweb values.
walkthrough: The selected constant is passed in HttpServer options.
Redweb installs the corresponding Express body parser.
Route handlers then read the parsed value from req.body.
article.watchFor: Body parsing is not schema validation. Limit body size and validate every field before using it.

api.name: METHODS
api.summary: Lowercase HTTP verb helpers passed straight to Express route registration.
api.usage:
import { METHODS } from 'redweb'
// METHODS.GET, METHODS.POST, METHODS.PUT, METHODS.DELETE

methods.name: GET
methods.detail: Use with services array or Express: METHODS.GET

methods.name: POST
methods.detail: Use with services array or Express: METHODS.POST

methods.name: PUT
methods.detail: Use with services array or Express: METHODS.PUT

methods.name: DELETE
methods.detail: Use with services array or Express: METHODS.DELETE

article.eli5: METHODS is a spelling-safe list of HTTP verbs—the labels on requests that say whether they read, create, replace, change, or delete something.
article.useWhen: Use it in Redweb service definitions to avoid scattered uppercase strings and accidental unsupported verbs.
walkthrough: A service definition pairs its path with a METHODS value.
BaseHttpServer registers the matching Express operation.
Requests with another verb do not accidentally invoke that service.
article.watchFor: The HTTP verb is only one part of API semantics. Implement authentication, idempotency, validation, and appropriate status codes in the service.

api.name: BaseSocketServer
api.summary: Shared lifecycle and route-composition base for SocketServer and SecureSocketServer. Prefer defineApp for application startup; use concrete server classes or this base for infrastructure integrations.

methods.name: addRoute(RouteClass)
methods.detail: Creates and registers one route class while enforcing unique paths.

methods.name: beginDrain()
methods.detail: Stops accepting new upgrades across every registered route.

methods.name: shutdown()
methods.detail: Drains routes and closes owned listeners without closing caller-owned servers.

article.eli5: BaseSocketServer is the engine room beneath both plain and secure socket servers. It coordinates routes and upgrades without deciding how the outer listener was created.
article.useWhen: Use this advanced surface for custom integrations that need Redweb routing on a specially managed Node HTTP or HTTPS server.
walkthrough: Your application supplies or prepares the listener.
BaseSocketServer attaches bounded WebSocket upgrade and route lifecycle behavior.
Concrete server ownership remains visible, including whether Redweb may listen or close it.
article.watchFor: Most applications should use defineApp. Reach for lower-level servers only when listener ownership needs a custom integration.

api.name: LiveHtmlServer
api.summary: Lower-level server-rendered page host. Prefer defineApp({ pages, sockets }) and app.run() to compose a new application; LiveHtmlServer remains available for direct page-host lifecycle integration.
api.usage:
import { LiveHtmlServer } from 'redweb'
import { DocsPage, StatusPage } from './pages.js'

const server = new LiveHtmlServer({
  pages: [DocsPage, StatusPage],
  port: 8080,
  heartbeat: { intervalMs: 15_000, timeoutMs: 10_000 },
})
options: pages: non-empty array of classes decorated with page()
templateRoot: optional root for colocated HTML and CSS assets
sessionTtlMs and maxSessions: bound pending and reconnectable sessions
maxConcurrentRenders: independent HTTP render concurrency ceiling
heartbeat: detects half-open browser connections
authenticate: binds HTTP renders and socket upgrades to one stable identity
origins: exact allowlist or asynchronous origin predicate

methods.name: constructor(options)
methods.detail: Builds the page renderer, HTTP routes, generated assets, and live WebSocket route on one listener.

methods.name: shutdown()
methods.detail: Aborts active renders, drains routes, disposes pages and components, and closes owned resources.

article.eli5: LiveHtmlServer is a stage manager for server-rendered pages. It serves the first complete HTML scene, then carries approved actions backstage and sends updated pieces back.
article.useWhen: Use defineApp for the normal application entry point. Construct LiveHtmlServer directly only when you need to own its lower-level listener and shutdown behavior.
walkthrough: HTTP rendering creates complete HTML and binds a stable page identity.
The generated live socket accepts only declared actions for that page.
State changes produce bounded updates while authentication and resource limits cover both transports.
article.watchFor: Decide deliberately whether page state is per connection or shared. Authenticate both HTTP and upgrade paths with the same identity and cap render concurrency.

api.name: LivePage and start
api.summary: Pages are plain decorated classes; extending LivePage is optional. Prefer defineApp({ pages: [...] }) and app.run() for startup. start() remains a supported lower-level convenience.

methods.name: start(PageClass, options?)
methods.detail: Starts one decorated page, or an array of pages, with the concise Live HTML server API.

methods.name: loading(context)
methods.detail: Optional cancellable hook that runs before the initial server render.

methods.name: connected(context)
methods.detail: Optional hook that runs after the authenticated live socket connects.

methods.name: disconnected(context)
methods.detail: Optional hook for stopping connection-owned timers and subscriptions.

methods.name: disposed()
methods.detail: Optional idempotent final cleanup hook for pages and components.

article.eli5: A page class describes one server-owned screen. defineApp groups the screens and socket routes; run opens their shared front door.
article.useWhen: Use a plain @page class for route-owned state, actions and rendering. LivePage inheritance and start remain compatibility options, not requirements.
walkthrough: @page declares the HTTP route and page policy.
@state reads in TSX update automatically; no output wrapper or repeated binding name is required.
defineApp registers the page, and app.run starts it. The example uses shared state deliberately so two tabs see the same counter.
article.watchFor: Keep constructors cheap and use lifecycle hooks for cancellable work. Connection-scoped state is the default; shared state is public to all authorized visitors of that page.

api.name: page, component, state, action, view
api.summary: Small TypeScript decorators declare routes, reusable component ownership, reactive server state, browser-callable actions, and collection item views.

methods.name: page(path, options?)
methods.detail: Registers a unique route plus template, CSS, sharing, metadata, caching, and live/static behavior.

methods.name: component()
methods.detail: Marks a class as a reusable state/action/lifecycle namespace.

methods.name: component(render)
methods.detail: Creates a concise synchronous function component for stateless reusable HTML.

methods.name: state(options?)
methods.detail: Publishes reassigned values; writable state may also receive bounded browser input.

methods.name: action({ input? })
methods.detail: Explicitly exposes one method to rw-click or rw-submit. An optional Standard Schema input validates and transforms one submitted argument before invocation; ActionInput<typeof schema> describes its output. Invalid input stays recoverable, while validator bugs remain server failures. Undecorated methods stay unreachable.

methods.name: rw-status="action"
methods.detail: Optional component-scoped placement for built-in action feedback. Without a slot, buttons/forms get an automatic status message. Pending duplicates from one control are suppressed; late responses preserve changed drafts and replacement forms. Disconnected actions are never queued or replayed.

methods.name: view(stateName)
methods.detail: Renders each item of one decorated array for an rw-each collection.

article.eli5: The decorators are small labels: page says where a screen lives, component says what can be reused, state says what may change, action says what the browser may request, and view describes repeated items.
article.useWhen: Use them to make server-rendered ownership visible next to the class member it affects instead of maintaining a separate routing and binding manifest.
walkthrough: @page registers the outer route and page policy.
@state and @action expose only explicitly declared reactive behavior.
The counter renders ordinary TSX over its state; changes reach both tabs because the page explicitly opts into shared state. Use the chat recipe to explore reusable class components.
article.watchFor: Decorators are an allow-list, not decoration. Keep actions narrow, validate their arguments, and avoid exposing arbitrary method invocation.

api.name: JSX rendering
api.summary: Dependency-free server-side TSX that renders directly to HtmlFragment values. It provides readable components, fragments, arrays, automatic escaping, safe attributes, and existing html-fragment interoperability without React, a virtual DOM, or hydration.
options: TypeScript: jsx = react-jsx and jsxImportSource = redweb
Production runtime: redweb/jsx-runtime; development runtime: redweb/jsx-dev-runtime
External CSS and rw-* server directives replace inline styles and browser event functions

methods.name: Intrinsic elements
methods.detail: Serialize standard, SVG, custom, data-*, aria-*, and rw-* attributes with HTML-correct boolean handling.

methods.name: Fragments and arrays
methods.detail: Compose nested fragments and readonly child arrays without wrapper markup or comma coercion.

methods.name: Function components
methods.detail: Synchronous functions receive typed props and children and must return an HtmlFragment or fragment array.

methods.name: Escaping and URLs
methods.detail: Text and attributes escape automatically; URL attributes retain Redweb’s safe-protocol validation.

methods.name: Interoperability
methods.detail: Existing html fragments nest in TSX and TSX fragments nest in html for incremental migration.

article.eli5: Redweb JSX is a readable HTML-shaped pencil. It turns TSX into safe server HTML directly—there is no React engine or browser copy hiding behind it.
article.useWhen: Use it whenever nested template strings become difficult to read or reusable server-rendered components make page structure clearer.
walkthrough: npx redweb init supplies the redweb/tsconfig.json preset. Save JSX source as .tsx; no React dependency or extra component wrapper is required.
Text and attributes are escaped while fragments, arrays, and components are flattened predictably.
The resulting HtmlFragment works with static pages and Live HTML without hydration.
article.watchFor: JSX is syntax, not automatic client reactivity. Only Live HTML state and actions create a realtime channel; static-site TSX remains zero-runtime HTML.

api.name: html, attribute, url, each, codeBlock
api.summary: Safe composition primitives escape text and quoted primitive attributes by default. URL attributes additionally reject executable, protocol-relative, and malformed values. Arrays must contain trusted HtmlFragment values.
api.usage: import { codeBlock, each, html } from 'redweb' const links = sections.map(section => ({ id: section.id, href: `#${section.id}`, label: section.name, })) const navigation = each(links, link => html` ${link.label} `) const example = codeBlock(source, { language: 'ts', label: 'TypeScript', highlight: highlightTypeScript, })

methods.name: html`...`
methods.detail: Creates an HtmlFragment and escapes every ordinary interpolation.

methods.name: attribute(value)
methods.detail: Optionally brands a primitive for a quoted, non-URL attribute when explicit intent improves readability.

methods.name: url(value)
methods.detail: Optionally brands a safe relative, HTTP, HTTPS, mail, or telephone URL; direct strings receive the same validation.

methods.name: each(items, render)
methods.detail: Validates and joins a mutable or readonly list of HtmlFragment results.

methods.name: codeBlock(code, options?)
methods.detail: Builds an escaped figure/pre/code fragment and can invoke a safe server-side highlighter.

article.eli5: These helpers are different safety tools: html builds trusted structure, attribute and url escape risky contexts, each joins lists, and codeBlock displays code without executing it.
article.useWhen: Use them for low-level templates, dynamic attributes, URLs, collections, and code samples when JSX is not the clearest representation.
walkthrough: Untrusted values are passed through the helper matching their HTML context.
HtmlFragment values preserve the distinction between approved markup and ordinary text.
Collection and code helpers produce predictable escaped output without hand-built concatenation.
article.watchFor: Escaping is context-specific. Never treat an escaped attribute as a safe URL or mark user-provided HTML as trusted.

api.name: defineSite
api.summary: Defines shared static-site CSS, metadata, caching, layout, canonical URLs, and export behavior once. Site pages are always runtime-free.
options: origin: optional HTTP(S) origin used to derive canonical and root-relative social-image URLs
css, head, cache, and layout: defaults inherited by every site.page() decorator
layout: synchronous function receiving the trusted page fragment and portable request context
publicDir: optional link-free asset tree staged with generated output

methods.name: site.page(path, options?)
methods.detail: Creates a non-live page decorator while merging shared defaults and page-specific overrides.

methods.name: site.export(pageOrPages, options)
methods.detail: Stages all pages and public assets, rejects path collisions, then writes the destination and returns every output path.

article.eli5: defineSite is the shared blueprint for a collection of pages: one place for the frame, colors, metadata, cache policy, canonical links, and export rules.
article.useWhen: Use it for documentation, marketing, or content sites where many runtime-free pages should share layout and production behavior.
walkthrough: The site definition establishes origin, common CSS, head metadata, cache policy, and layout.
Decorated pages contribute their own route, title, description, and stylesheet.
site.export stages every page and asset into one consistent static output.
article.watchFor: The layout must handle every exported route. Keep route-specific chrome derived from stable metadata rather than scattered path checks.

api.name: exportStatic
api.summary: Renders non-live decorated pages to deterministic directory indexes and content-addressed CSS. It is intended for docs, marketing pages, and static hosting.
options: outDir: required output directory; existing unrelated files are preserved
templateRoot: optional explicit root for templates and CSS
logger: optional framework logger or null

methods.name: exportStatic(pageOrPages, options)
methods.detail: Returns frozen page and asset path lists after every page renders and its CSS is written.

article.eli5: exportStatic is a printing press: give it pages, and it writes finished HTML and assets that any ordinary static host can serve.
article.useWhen: Use it when you need direct static export without defining a reusable site object and its shared layout policy.
walkthrough: Page metadata determines output routes and page assets.
exportStatic writes the requested output; your build owns any staging directory and atomic replacement.
The returned paths let build tooling audit or publish exactly what was produced.
article.watchFor: Export into a staging directory and replace the live build atomically. A failed render should never leave a partially updated site. This top-level await example uses an ESM build script; it never starts an HTTP server.

api.name: HtmlRenderer
api.summary: Lower-level rendering utility. Most applications should use plain @page classes with defineApp, or defineSite for static sites; this surface supports tooling and advanced integrations.

methods.name: render(source, page, options?)
methods.detail: Renders declarative bindings and collection views against a page object.

methods.name: document(markup, config?, stylesheets?, metadata?)
methods.detail: Wraps markup in a complete document and injects metadata, CSS, and optional live bootstrap.

methods.name: template() / stylesheet()
methods.detail: Loads a validated page asset inside an explicit root.

methods.name: statePayload()
methods.detail: Builds the text or trusted-HTML state payload used by live updates.

article.eli5: HtmlRenderer is the machinery under the hood that turns a page object and its declared bindings into final markup.
article.useWhen: Use it only for integrations that need lower-level rendering control; normal applications should prefer TSX pages with defineApp or defineSite.
walkthrough: A source template or fragment and page instance enter the renderer.
Declared state, actions, views, and safe values are resolved under the render options.
The caller receives final HTML suitable for its own response or build pipeline.
article.watchFor: The lower-level API gives you more lifecycle responsibility. Preserve escaping, cancellation, ownership, and bounded concurrency rather than rebuilding them casually.

api.name: defineSocketContract
api.summary: One shared Standard Schema contract validates wire payloads and infers client/server types. Route URLs choose the service; individual handler factories dispatch by message type.

methods.name: defineSocketContract(version, schemas, options?)
methods.detail: Creates an immutable contract and negotiated protocol policy from Standard Schema validators. Redweb does not require a particular validator at runtime.

methods.name: handler(type, callback)
methods.detail: Creates a BaseHandler subclass. Validation completes before the callback receives its typed payload. The returned class can bind rw-submit or rw-click on a socket-bound page; Handler.with(payload) snapshots typed input.

methods.name: client(socket)
methods.detail: Wraps an existing WebSocket with typed, validated send and parse methods. It does not open or reconnect the connection.

methods.name: send(socket, type, payload, metadata?)
methods.detail: Validates server output before sending through the normal transport and protocol policy.

article.eli5: A socket contract is a shared form for both sides of a conversation. It says which messages exist and what each message must contain, so the server checks a message before handing it to the matching handler.
article.useWhen: Use it when a site, app, or game client should share payload types and runtime validation with a routed Redweb service.
walkthrough: The shared module defines join, move, resume, and state payload schemas once.
The match route registers separate handlers created by the contract instead of switching on a secondary action field.
The client and server validate their outgoing messages and parse incoming envelopes against the same schema.
For server-rendered UI, attach the route through @page({ socket: Route }) and bind its handler classes directly to TSX. connectedClients can supply verified player facades and per-player projection.
article.watchFor: Schema validation is not authentication or game-rule validation. Keep bearer session IDs private, apply authorization in handlers, and persist important data outside the starter's bounded in-memory sessions. Async validation deadlines cannot preempt synchronous JavaScript.

api.name: connectedClients / ConnectedClient
api.summary: Route-owned connected players with checked identity, bounded room membership, deduplicated presence and private server-page updates. Reuses RoomRegistry; no second socket map or browser dispatcher is required.
options: identity: rechecks the admitted principal against current credentials
page: lazy reference to the attached page class
project: side-effect-free per-player page state; online identities are deduplicated
reject / errorState: classify deliberately public errors and map them to page fields
raw: optional update/reject adapters for non-HTML clients
authorizationTimeoutMs / projectionTimeoutMs: bounded asynchronous work

methods.name: players.bind(contract)
methods.detail: Creates typed handlers whose callback receives a ConnectedClient; successful commands refresh its rooms.

methods.name: players.get(socket)
methods.detail: Returns the checked route-owned facade for page connection lifecycle hooks.

methods.name: players.refresh(room)
methods.detail: Projects external domain changes to that room’s currently authorized connections.

methods.name: player.identity / page / rooms / room
methods.detail: Admitted identity, private page, membership snapshot, and exactly-one-room convenience accessor.

methods.name: player.join(room, commit?) / leave(room)
methods.detail: Checks capacity and authorization before a synchronous domain commit; failure removes newly added membership, not arbitrary domain side effects.

article.eli5: Each player gets a checked name badge and a private screen. Redweb tracks who is connected and updates their screens; your game still decides what each person may do and see.
article.useWhen: Use it with socket-bound TSX pages to remove manual membership maps, identity rechecks, presence loops and fan-out code. Ordinary raw socket routes need not adopt it.
walkthrough: Create a fresh group inside the application factory and register it with one SocketRoute.
Bind typed handlers and use their classes in TSX controls; connect the page to that route.
After successful commands and membership changes, Redweb projects each player’s permitted state and discards obsolete results.
article.watchFor: Create one group per route instance. Identity must match the admitted principal. Applications still own room authorization, game rules, transactions, seat recovery and persistence. Raw state events are uncorrelated; request completion uses redweb:result. Never send inside projection adapters.

examples.label: Private rooms
examples.title: One identity for a page and a protected room
examples.summary: A complete local demonstration of shared authentication, decorator-first server HTML and explicitly authorized raw socket room entry.
notes: Save this as src/app.tsx in an initialized realtime starter, build and start it. The printed token is a fresh local-demo credential; do not publish it or treat this as a production identity service.

Supply the Authorization header for GET / and the /team WebSocket, then send {"type":"join"}. Browser products should use a secure session/cookie integration; native browser WebSockets cannot set this header.
Both decorator modes and source-free production execution are checked with real HTTP/WebSockets. The example explicitly revokes raw room memberships as well as Live HTML page sessions.

examples.label: Start here
examples.title: HTTP and WebSockets on one listener
examples.summary: Register an Express endpoint and a socket route with defineApp. One run call starts their shared listener; the application owns shutdown.
notes: GET /health returns JSON; ws://127.0.0.1:8181/chat accepts {"type":"hello"}. The HTTP endpoint reports liveness, not readiness.
Use the complete http-ws starter for compiler configuration and actual HTTP/WebSocket tests. It binds loopback for local development.
Application shutdown closes both HTTP and socket resources. Configure authentication, trusted origins, limits and HTTPS/WSS before public deployment.

examples.label: Rendered UI
examples.title: Server state and reusable TSX components
examples.summary: Ordinary TSX expressions read server-owned state and update automatically after an action; no repeated binding names or browser component runtime.
notes: The first response is complete server-rendered HTML.
Function components handle stateless snippets; decorated classes own state and actions.
There is no React dependency, virtual DOM, or hydration pass.

examples.label: Static HTML
examples.title: A complete site with shared defaults
examples.summary: Define metadata, layout, CSS, caching, and asset export once, then keep each page focused on its content.
notes: Canonical URLs are derived from the route and origin.
Public assets and rendered pages are staged before output changes.
The generated site contains no Redweb browser runtime or WebSocket.

examples.label: Messages
examples.title: JSON routing, broadcast, and binary frames
examples.summary: Text messages select a handler by type. Binary frames stay as Buffer values and can be accepted by the handler that understands them.
notes: sendJson and broadcast share the same outbound policy.
acceptsBinary can select among multiple binary handlers.
Async handler failures become safe client errors.

examples.label: Production
examples.title: Bound admission, work, and slow peers
examples.summary: Production controls are opt-in and route-local. Authenticate before upgrade, cap every queue, and use one heartbeat scheduler for the whole route.
notes: Authentication completes before onInitialContact.
Ordered overflow closes pending work synchronously.
Disabled controls add no per-connection queue or timer.

examples.label: Players
examples.title: Match handlers and resumable ownership
examples.summary: Give the match its own socket route, then dispatch join, move and resume by type. These canonical socket-starter handlers create and recover server-owned player sessions; they are not a room-broadcast or account-authentication example.
notes: Initialize the complete socket recipe: src/contract.ts defines validated payloads and src/app.tsx configures /match, session capacity and transport limits. This file is not a standalone server.
Join issues a random bearer session token. Move requires an existing player; resume restores that player on a new connection and replaces the previous owner.
Keep the state response and session token private. Add account authentication and application movement rules before production; sessions remain in memory and expire 30 seconds after disconnect.
For authenticated group delivery, use the separate One identity for a page and a protected room example. The shared socket contracts guide links its complete source and the room-authorization guide.

examples.label: Simulation
examples.title: Fixed-step work without overlapping ticks
examples.summary: FixedStepService compensates for scheduler drift, bounds catch-up, contains async failures, and reports lag that was deliberately dropped.
notes: The active async tick must finish before another begins.
maxCatchUpTicks prevents a spiral of death.
maxRetainedLagMs bounds remembered delay.

examples.label: Clients
examples.title: Versioned envelopes with an explicitly owned connection
examples.summary: Negotiate a finite protocol version before upgrade, then share stable envelopes and error codes between server and client.
notes: Browsers negotiate with redwebVersion in the query.
requestId correlates; sequence expresses application ordering.
Neither field promises durability or exactly-once delivery.
ProtocolClient is the low-level envelope helper, not redweb-client. For generated server-TSX UI, bind typed handlers instead of writing this browser module.

examples.label: Multiple nodes
examples.title: Bring your own broker adapter
examples.summary: Redweb supplies a bounded composition seam rather than choosing infrastructure. Events are finite, deduplicated briefly, and explicitly best-effort.
notes: Required adapters affect readiness; best-effort adapters do not.
Source-node events are ignored to prevent reflection loops.
Authoritative state and partition reconciliation remain application work.

examples.label: Operations
examples.title: Readiness first, then bounded shutdown
examples.summary: Stop placement to the node, flip readiness, let cooperative handlers observe cancellation, and await deterministic cleanup.
notes: New upgrades receive 503 once draining starts.
Handlers on routes with drainHandlers: true receive cancellation through socket.context.signal; application work must cooperate.
A hard deadline terminates non-cooperating peers.
